grammar.explanation: 係 links a subject to a noun: who or what something is. It is not used before adjectives — say 佢好高 (he is tall), not 佢係高. To negate, use 唔係.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 是; in speech always say 係.

mistakes.note: 他 and 是 are written forms. Speech uses 佢 and 係.

grammar.explanation: Put 唔 directly before a verb or adjective to negate it. The one big exception is 有 (to have): its negative is 冇, never 唔有.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 不; in speech always say 唔.

mistakes.note: 不 is written Chinese. Say 唔.

grammar.meaning: to have; there is / there isn't
grammar.explanation: 有 means both 'to have' and 'there is'. Its negative is the single word 冇 — 唔有 is always wrong.

writtenEquivalent.note: 沒有 is written Chinese; in speech say 冇.

mistakes.note: The negative of 有 is 冇, not 唔有.

grammar.explanation: 有冇 ('have or not have') turns 有 into a question. Answer 有 for yes or 冇 for no. Ending with 呀 makes it sound friendly.
examples: Do you have an Octopus card?

grammar.explanation: The most natural way to ask a yes/no question is to say the verb, then 唔, then the verb again: 去唔去 ('go not go'). For two-syllable words, repeat only the first syllable: 好唔好食. Answer by repeating the verb: 去 or 唔去.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese tends to use 嗎 or 是否.

grammar.explanation: Add 咗 straight after a verb to show the action has happened or been completed. It often translates as an English past tense or 'have done'.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 了; in speech say 咗.

mistakes.note: 吃 and 了 are written forms. Speech uses 食 and 咗.

grammar.explanation: Add 緊 straight after a verb to say an action is happening right now, like English '-ing'.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 正在 before the verb.

grammar.explanation: 嘅 joins an owner or a description to a noun: 我嘅書 (my book), 好食嘅餐廳 (a good restaurant). With family and close friends it is usually dropped: 我媽媽, 我朋友.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 的; in speech say 嘅.

examples: I know a really good restaurant.

mistakes.note: 這 and 的 are written forms. Speech uses 呢 + classifier and 嘅.

grammar.explanation: 喺 (hai2) says where someone or something is, or where an action happens. Don't confuse it with 係 (hai6, 'to be') — only the tone is different.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 在; in speech say 喺.

mistakes.note: 在 and 哪裏 are written forms. Speech uses 喺 and 邊度.

grammar.explanation: 呢 (this) and 嗰 (that) always need a classifier after them: 呢個, 嗰件, 呢間. The noun can be dropped when it's obvious from context.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 這 and 那.

examples: I'd like that one (piece of clothing).

grammar.explanation: A number cannot go straight before a noun: a classifier goes in between. 個 is the general one; others depend on the noun's shape or type (杯 cups, 本 books, 部 machines). Use 兩 (loeng5), not 二, for 'two' before a classifier.
examples: I want to buy a new phone.

mistakes.note: Before a classifier, 'two' is 兩, not 二.

grammar.explanation: 想 before a verb says what you would like to do. It is softer and more polite than 要.
examples: Where would you like to go?

grammar.meaning: to want (something); to need to / have to
grammar.explanation: 要 + noun is how you order or ask for things. 要 + verb means 'need to' or 'have to'. Its negative, 唔要, means 'don't want'; 'don't need to' is 唔使.
examples: One bowl of wonton noodles, please.

grammar.explanation: Adjectives work like verbs, so no 係 is needed. A bare adjective can sound incomplete or comparative, so 好 is added by default — it often means just 'is' rather than a strong 'very'.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 很; in speech say 好.

mistakes.note: 很 is written Chinese. 'Very good' is 好好.

grammar.explanation: Put 幾多錢 after the thing you are asking about. Prices are answered with a number + 蚊 (man1, dollars): 三十蚊.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 多少.

examples: How much is a milk tea?
How much is it to the airport?

mistakes.note: 這 and 多少 are written forms.

grammar.explanation: 乜嘢 means 'what' and stays in the same place as the answer would: 你食乜嘢？ — 我食飯. 咩 (me1) is the short, everyday form.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 甚麼 / 什麼.

grammar.pattern: 邊度 / 邊個 / 邊 + Classifier
grammar.jyutping: bin1 dou6 / bin1 go3 / bin1 + Classifier
grammar.explanation: 邊 means 'which'. 邊度 is 'which place' (where), 邊個 is 'which person' (who), and 邊 + any classifier asks 'which one': 邊件, 邊間.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 哪裏, 誰 and 哪.

grammar.explanation: 幾時 goes before the verb, where the time word would go in the answer: 你幾時返工？ — 我九點返工.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 甚麼時候.

examples: When do you go to work?
When did you come to Hong Kong?

grammar.meaning: friendly softener for questions and replies
grammar.explanation: Sentence-final particles add tone of voice. 呀 makes questions and short answers sound warm rather than blunt. 你去邊度？ is abrupt; 你去邊度呀？ is friendly.
啦 (laa1, high level tone) turns a statement into a suggestion or polite urging: 'let's…', 'go ahead and…'. Don't confuse it with 喇 (laa3), which marks a change of situation.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 吧.

mistakes.note: 我們 and 吧 are written forms. Speech uses 我哋 and 啦.

grammar.explanation: Adding 嗎 to a statement makes it a yes/no question. It is correct and widely understood, though A-not-A questions (去唔去？) sound more colloquial in everyday speech.
同 joins two nouns ('and') or says who you do something with ('with'). It joins nouns and people, not whole sentences.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 和 or 跟.

examples: I'm going to see a film with her.
One milk tea and one coffee, please.

grammar.explanation: 唔好 before a verb tells someone not to do something. It is the everyday way to say 'don't'. Compare 唔使, which means 'there's no need to'.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 不要 or 別.

mistakes.note: 不要 is written Chinese. Say 唔好.

grammar.explanation: 定係 (often shortened to 定) offers a choice in a question: tea or coffee? In a statement, 'or' is 或者 instead.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 還是.

examples: Would you like tea or coffee?
Is she a teacher or a student?

mistakes.note: 還是 is written Chinese; 或者 is for statements, not questions.

grammar.pattern: Verb + 咗 + … 未？ / 未 + Verb
grammar.explanation: Put 未 at the end of a 咗 sentence to ask 'yet?'. Answer …咗喇 (yes, already) or 未呀 (not yet). Before a verb, 未 means 'haven't yet'. 食咗飯未呀？ is also an everyday greeting.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 了沒有 and 還沒.

grammar.explanation: 過 after a verb says you have had the experience at some point: 'have been to', 'have tried'. 未 + Verb + 過 means 'have never'.
examples: Have you ever tried yuenyeung (coffee with milk tea)?

grammar.meaning: know how to; can (a learned skill)
grammar.explanation: 識 before a verb means you have learned how to do something: speak a language, swim, drive. For learned skills it is more natural than 會, which leans towards 'will'.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 會 for learned ability.

examples: I can speak a little Cantonese.

mistakes.note: 不, 會 and 說 are written forms. Speech uses 唔識講.

grammar.explanation: 可以 means 'may' or 'can' (permission or possibility). Its A-not-A form 可唔可以 is the standard polite request. Answer 可以 (yes) or 唔可以 (no).
examples: Could you make it a bit cheaper?
Could you speak a bit more slowly?

grammar.explanation: 太 before an adjective means 'too'. It is very often followed by 喇, which marks the situation as having gone past what's acceptable.
點解 can go at the start of the question or after the subject. Answers usually begin with 因為 (because). Ending with 㗎 adds a note of puzzlement.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 為甚麼.

grammar.explanation: 點 or 點樣 before a verb asks how to do it. 點去…？ ('how to get to…?') is essential for directions.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 怎樣 / 怎麼.

examples: Excuse me, how do I get to Central?
What's the fastest way to the airport?
How do you pronounce this character?

grammar.explanation: 喇 (laa3, mid level tone) signals that something has changed or a new situation now holds: I'm full now, it's started raining. Compare 啦 (laa1), which makes suggestions.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses sentence-final 了.

grammar.explanation: At the end of a sentence, 咩 shows surprise or doubt: you expected the opposite. 你識講廣東話咩？ means 'You can speak Cantonese?!' This is different from 咩 meaning 'what' inside a sentence.
都 means 'also' or 'all' and always goes before the verb — never at the end of the sentence like English 'too'. With a negative, 都唔 means 'not … either'.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese often uses 也.

mistakes.note: 都 goes before the verb, not at the end.

grammar.explanation: 畀 means 'give'. In traditional Cantonese order the thing comes before the person: 畀杯水我 ('give a glass of water me'). The Mandarin-like order 畀我… is also heard, especially among younger speakers.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 給, with the person first.

examples: Could I have a glass of water, please?

mistakes.note: 他, 給 and 了 are written forms.

grammar.explanation: 吓 after a verb softens it: 'have a quick look', 'give it a try', 'wait a moment'. It makes requests and suggestions sound relaxed.
examples: Let me have a look first.

grammar.explanation: To compare, put 過 after the adjective: 佢高過我 ('he tall-past me'). The written-style 佢比我高 is understood, but 過 is the natural spoken form.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 比 before the adjective.

examples: The MTR is faster than the bus.

mistakes.note: 他 is written; 比 sounds bookish in casual speech.

grammar.explanation: 因為 introduces the reason and 所以 the result. Unlike English, using both in one sentence is normal. Either half can also stand alone.
examples: Because it was raining, I didn't go out.
I'm tired because I went to bed late last night.
Because she's ill, she isn't going to work today.

grammar.explanation: Instead of 嘅, Cantonese often joins an owner to a specific thing with its classifier: 我部手機 is 'my phone', 佢間屋 is 'her flat'. This is very common in everyday speech.
examples: Her flat is in Sha Tin.

grammar.explanation: 會 before a verb talks about the future or what is likely: it will rain, I'll call you. 唔會 means 'won't' or 'is unlikely to'.
應該 gives advice ('you should') or a reasonable guess ('she should be there by now').
examples: You should go to bed earlier.
She should have arrived by now.

grammar.meaning: no need to; don't have to
grammar.explanation: 唔使 says something isn't necessary. It is the negative of 要 ('need to'). Don't confuse it with 唔好, which tells someone not to do something.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 不用.

examples: You're welcome. (No need to be polite.)
I don't have to go to work today.
You don't need to pay — it's free.

grammar.explanation: 完 after a verb means the action is finished: 做完 (finish doing), 食完 (finish eating). It often comes with 咗 or 喇.
examples: I'll go to bed when I've finished this film.

grammar.explanation: 已經 goes before the verb, and the sentence usually ends with 喇 to mark the new situation.
examples: It's already ten o'clock — hurry up!

grammar.explanation: 到 (dou2, rising tone) after a verb says the action succeeded: 搵到 (found), 買到 (managed to buy). Put 唔 in between for 'couldn't': 買唔到. This is a different word from 到 (dou3) 'to arrive'.

grammar.meaning: how well / how fast someone does something
grammar.explanation: To describe how an action is done, put 得 after the verb and then the description: 行得好慢 (walks slowly). If the verb has an object, say the verb twice: 講廣東話講得好好.
晒 after a verb means the action covers everything: 賣晒 (sold out), 食晒 (ate it all). 唔該晒 and 多謝晒 mean 'thanks very much'.
examples: The egg tarts are sold out.

grammar.meaning: back; again; return to a previous state
grammar.explanation: 返 after a verb means getting something back or returning to how things were: 攞返 (take back), 還返 (give back), 好返 (get better).
examples: I'd like to get my umbrella back.
When will you give the book back to me?

grammar.pattern: Verb + 出 / 入 / 上 / 落 + 嚟 / 去
grammar.jyutping: Verb + ceot1 / jap6 / soeng5 / lok6 + lai4 / heoi3
grammar.explanation: 嚟 means towards the speaker and 去 away from the speaker. Add 出 (out), 入 (in), 上 (up) or 落 (down) for the direction, and they can follow another verb: 行出去 (walk out).
To say something was done to someone, use 畀 followed by who did it. If you don't know who, use 畀人 ('by someone'). Spoken Cantonese never uses written 被 here.

writtenEquivalent.note: Written Chinese uses 被.

examples: I got told off by my boss.
My little brother ate all the cake.

mistakes.note: 的, 錢包, 被 and 了 are written forms.

grammar.explanation: 如果 introduces the condition and 就 the result. 就 goes after the subject of the second half, before the verb.
examples: If it rains tomorrow, we won't go.
If you're free, come to my place for dinner.
If you don't understand, you can ask me.

grammar.explanation: 雖然 introduces a contrast and 但係 the main point. Unlike English, both words are normally used in the same sentence.
examples: Although she was busy, she still came.
Although I've studied for two years, I still don't speak well.

grammar.explanation: 一 before the first verb and 就 before the second link two events closely: as soon as one happens, the other follows.
examples: I'll call you as soon as I arrive.
He goes home as soon as he finishes work.
Whenever I drink coffee, I can't sleep.

grammar.explanation: 越嚟越 before an adjective describes something that keeps increasing: hotter and hotter, better and better.
examples: The weather's getting hotter and hotter.
Your Cantonese is getting better and better!
Flats in Hong Kong are getting more and more expensive.

grammar.explanation: 先 means 'first' and 再 'then'. Very typically for Cantonese, 先 can also come at the end of a sentence: 等我諗吓先 (let me think first).
examples: Let's eat first, then go to the cinema.
Do your homework first, then play.
Let me think about it first.

grammar.explanation: 囉 at the end of a sentence presents something as obvious or the natural conclusion, sometimes with a shrug: 'well, then…', 'of course'.
examples: If you don't like it, just don't eat it.

grammar.meaning: noticing something; passing on what someone said
grammar.explanation: 喎 marks something you have just noticed ('oh, look…') or information you are passing on from someone else ('he said…').
examples: Wow, there are so many people!
He says he's not coming today.
Hey, this restaurant's actually pretty good.

grammar.explanation: To describe a noun with a whole phrase, put the phrase first, then 嘅, then the noun: 我尋日買嘅衫 ('the top I bought yesterday'). English puts the description after the noun; Cantonese puts it before.
examples: The top I bought yesterday was cheap.
She's the teacher who teaches me Cantonese.
Is there anything to eat that isn't spicy?

grammar.meaning: keep doing; in a continuing state
grammar.explanation: 住 after a verb describes an ongoing state rather than an action in progress: 戴住眼鏡 (wearing glasses), 攞住 (holding). Compare 緊, which describes an action happening now.
examples: Hold on to it for now.

grammar.meaning: seems; looks like; to be like
grammar.explanation: 好似 means 'seems' before a description, or 'to be like' before a noun: 佢好似唔開心 (she seems unhappy), 你好似你爸爸 (you look like your dad).
examples: It looks like it's going to rain.

words.en: thank you (for a service); excuse me
words.note: Use for small favours and services; 多謝 is for gifts and compliments.

words.en: thank you (for a gift or compliment)
you're welcome; no need to be polite

words.jyutping: hou2 gou1 hing3 jing6 sik1 nei5

words.en: Happy Lunar New Year (lit. wishing you prosperity)

words.note: Cantonese has no single word for 'yes'; people usually repeat the verb, or say 係 to confirm a fact.

words.en: take care (said to a guest who is leaving)

words.note: Use 兩 before classifiers (兩個) and 二 when counting or in larger numbers (二十).
Some people avoid 四 because it sounds like 死 (sei2, 'to die').
Considered lucky because it rhymes with 發 (faat3, 'to prosper').
Usually jyu2 when talking about fish as food; jyu4 in more formal words.
Same syllable as 買 but tone 6. Tone changes the meaning.

words.en: underground railway; the MTR (older everyday name)
to go through the ticket gate
to exit through the ticket gate
getting off, please! (said to a minibus driver)
uncle; polite term for an older man
auntie; polite term for an older woman
older male cousin (on the mother's side, or a father's sister's son)
to knock off; finish for the day

words.note: When it is raised, offices and schools close.

words.en: at a loss; frustrated (lit. itchy head)

vocabulary.title: Tech and work
vocabulary.note: Hong Kong office speech mixes in English words freely. The English words keep their English spelling here and are said much as in English, usually fitted to Cantonese rhythm. The fully Cantonese word is often more formal or written.

words.en: to have a bug; for a bug to appear

words.note: 執 means to tidy up or sort out.

words.en: to rush to meet a deadline

words.note: The same as 開會, and very common in offices.
OT is overtime, said as two letters; the same as 加班.

words.en: to be in charge of a project; to follow a project
to go in to the office
to go live; to launch online

words.note: Formal; in speech many developers simply say deploy.

words.en: to switch on (a computer or phone)
to switch off (a computer or phone)
to crash; to freeze (of a device)

path.title: Meeting people
path.goal: Greet people, say who you are, and ask simple yes-or-no questions.

dialogue.title: Nice to meet you
lines: Hi! I'm Ka-yan. What's your name?
Hi, I'm Tom. Nice to meet you!

path.title: Numbers and prices
path.goal: Count things, point at them, and ask what they cost and whether there are any.

dialogue.title: At the fruit stall
lines: Excuse me, do you have any apples?
Ten dollars each, or three for twenty-five.
I'll have three. Do you have any oranges?

path.title: Eating out
path.goal: Order food and drink, say what you want, and choose between options.

dialogue.title: Breakfast at a cha chaan teng
lines: What would you like to eat?
I'd like a pineapple bun and a bowl of wonton noodles.

path.title: Family and friends
path.goal: Talk about the people in your life and describe them.

dialogue.title: A family photo
lines: She's my older sister. She's very tall.
She lives in Sha Tin with her husband.
Yes, a son and a daughter.
Do you like being an auntie?
I love it! They're so cute.

path.title: Getting around
path.goal: Say where you are, when you are going, and what you have done or are doing.

dialogue.title: Meeting at the station
lines: I'm on the bus; I'm nearly there.
About ten minutes. Wait for me at the station.
OK. I'm here now, at Exit B.
Don't wander off — I'll be there as soon as I get off.

path.title: Shopping
path.goal: Compare things, say something is too dear, and ask if you may try or pay.

dialogue.title: Trying on clothes
lines: Could I try this top on?
Of course — the fitting room is over there.
It's too small. Do you have a bigger one?
Yes, this one's a large. The blue one looks better than the black.
It fits perfectly. How much is it?
Three hundred dollars, with 20% off today.
Great, I'll take it. Here's my card.
Thank you — your card and your receipt.

path.title: Asking the way
path.goal: Ask how to get somewhere and why, and say what you know how to do.

dialogue.title: The way to the Star Ferry
lines: Excuse me, how do I get to the Star Ferry pier?
Go straight on, past two sets of traffic lights, then turn left.
Not far, about five minutes on foot. Can you read a map?
Yes. Let me have a look.
Why are there so many people today?

path.title: Daily life
path.goal: Describe your day: what you have finished, what you have not done yet, and what you have ever done.

dialogue.title: Dinner at home
lines: Not yet. I've just finished work.
I've already cooked — let's eat together.
Steamed fish and vegetables. Have you ever had steamed fish?
When we've finished, you do the washing-up.

path.title: Seeing a doctor
path.goal: Describe how you feel, give reasons, and understand advice.

dialogue.title: At the clinic
lines: What seems to be the problem?
I've got a headache, and my throat hurts too.
No. I have to work tomorrow, so I want to get better quickly.
You've got a cold. You should rest for two days.
I don't have to go to work?
No, I'll write you a sick note.

path.title: At work
path.goal: Talk about tasks and results, how well things went, and what to do first.

dialogue.title: A bug before the meeting
lines: Have you finished the report yet?
It's all done — I've just sent it to you.
The system's got a bug. As soon as I've fixed it, I'll send it to you again.
Never mind. Go to the meeting first, then fix it.
By the way, you presented really well yesterday.

path.title: Weather and plans
path.goal: Make plans that depend on the weather, and talk about changes and impressions.

dialogue.title: Hiking or shopping?
lines: The Observatory says it's going to rain tomorrow.
If it rains, let's go to a shopping centre instead.
OK. It seems to be getting more and more humid today.
Yes. Although it's hot, I still want to go out for a walk.
Then come down — I'll wait for you downstairs.
Hang on, let me grab an umbrella first.

path.title: Telling stories
path.goal: Tell what happened and how you felt, react to news, and describe people and things in detail.

dialogue.title: A stolen wallet
lines: Why do you look so unhappy?
My wallet was stolen on the MTR this morning.
That's awful! How much money was in it?
Not much money, but the wallet my mum gave me is gone.
Did you report it to the police?
Yes. I'm sure I was holding my bag the whole time.
The MTR is so crowded — you just have to be careful.
True. Next time I'll wear it on my front.
